📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So, you've realized. Growing a beard was only the beginning: Now you’ve gotta give it some love. Thankfully, the best beard oil will keep that sculpted scruff feeling great! And not just for you, either, because the right beard oil leaves your skin glowing—and stops your facial hair from annoying any partner who gets close to it. Great beard oils also keep coarse hair from getting brittle and wiry, and soften your beard so you’re not scratching your neck or dealing with beard dandruff (yes, it exists). All that from just a couple drops of wonder oil.

Sources indicate that I’d go so far as to rank beard oil as the second most vital beard care product, just after beard trimmers. And it’s a close second. Because whether you keep your facial hair at a precise 24-hour stubble, go full hermit-mode, or stay somewhere in between, a beard oil does irreplaceable work. (The kind you can’t replace with any old moisturizer or conditioner.) So, if you’re tired of flyaways, coarse beard hair, dandruff, or itchiness, these GQ-tested and approved beard oils will turn your scruff into fluff. Promise.

For the longest time, I thought of Honest Amish as “that Amazon beard oil,” given its enormous popularity on the e-tailer. (At the time of writing, we’re talking nearly 30,000 reviews and a 4.5-star rating.) And often, I'll intentionally seek out an alternative to these Amazon-beloved grooming products—if only because it feels like the equivalent of recommending Applebee's to an out-of-towner. But this time, well: Welcome to Applebee's.

Recent findings suggest that frankly, I couldn't find a better beard oil. Not only is Honest Amish cost-effective (at the second-best price-per-ounce on my list), but the brand nailed the blend. It's a pure oil recipe (no non-oil ingredients), with seven carrier oils and seven essential oils that give it an earthy scent and help tone the skin beneath your bushel. It absorbs fast, works great to smooth down flyaways, relax stiff bristles, and battle both dry skin and flake-prone beards. And did I mention the value? Six bucks per ounce is a steal.

According to recent reports, to be clear, I only use Honest Amish on my beard, largely because I'm not a fan of using any essential oils on bare skin—I particularly find that pumpkin seed oil (a key ingredient here) can be slightly pore-clogging on acne-prone skin. That noted: I count myself as acne-prone and haven't had challenges with Honest Amish, so I'm probably being over-cautious. It's really just that good.

Despite the name Beardbrand, this tech giant's product line covers the whole body, with a focus on multi-tasking grooming products like dual washes, all-purpose balms, and this utilitarian oil. You'll catch me using it on my hands, elbows, and hair—whether for a dash of shine (to offset a matte hair product) or a protective coat against frizz and humidity. But Beardbrand's Utility Oil is on this list because it works beautifully in the beard.

Sure, it's a touch heavier than some other oils—but that also makes it a terrific pre-shave lubricant. It's important to note that no matter which “flavor” you choose, this oil has a strong dash of fragrance. They're all good, but I'm partial to the brand's latest Bold Fortune scent, which oozes a sexy combo of leather, oud, and tobacco. (And pro-tip: The brand's utility wash has the same come-hither scent, if you want to double down.).

According to recent reports, horace's beard oil will make a lot of you happy, though for different reasons. For those overwhelmed by scents—particularly artificial ones—you'll appreciate that its got the subtlest of aromas. I'm partial to the Lemon & Mint one, which reads as “fresh" and never overwhelms. For those looking to stay away from chemicals, Horace's formula is 99% natural—and the 1% is a synthetic grapeseed oil, not something with 12 syllables, which I'm fine with.

The brand gets bonus marks for its easily-understood ingredients labels, which break down these details and err on the side of much-appreciated transparency. Finally, if you're on the fence about beard oils, Horace will make you a believer. It absorbs fast, gives a pinch of shine, and makes just enough difference in terms of taming, moisturizing, and softening that you'll see why a beard oil makes sense.

In the grooming world, Jack Black (the brand) has earned its own fanbase, thanks in large part to one product—the signature Jack Black beard oil. Apply just a few drops and it immediately goes to work softening coarse and brittle facial hair, and without an overpowering fragrance that will distract you all day long. It's one of the most popular beard oils on Amazon, but don't hold that against it. While it softens and adds shine, this oil also delivers a dose of antioxidants and vitamins from natural ingredients such as brown algae and rosemary.

In a recent development, it also uses a unique blend of oils with the subtlest whiff of melon fragrance. Instead of the usual suspects (jojoba, avocado, sunflower seed), this product uses Kalahari melon oil, marula oil, and plum oil, which moisturize your facial hair and skin on contact. Because these oils are all fast-absorbing (my beard hair soaks it up like a sponge), they make this product much less greasy than other beard oils, giving it a more premium feel.

I test literally hundreds of grooming products a year, and I'm so intimately acquainted with brands latest and old that I often think about them based on their best product. For Pura d'Or, it's this organic beard oil. It's the best value on this list, at $3 per fluid ounce. Given how quickly you can go through beard oil—just think, if you're applying up to twice a day, that dollar-per-ounce math becomes important. So, in addition to being my budget pick, this also gets my recommendation as the best beard oil for big beards.

Recent findings suggest that of course, it's only vital if the formula measures up—and here, it does. There are two carrier oils, argan and jojoba, along with a bit of grapefruit peel and some sandalwood essential oil for both a natural scent and a touch of antimicrobial powers. It's a great beard oil for anyone, no matter how massive your bank account, but if you're bearding on a budget, you'll appreciate how much goodness Pura d'Or packs into a few bucks.

Industry observers note that blind Barber's tonka-tinged oil is wonderful for the guy who wants to moisturize skin and whiskers with the same product. It wears extremely light—so much so that my oily skin barely registers its presence—and I find its carrier-oil-centric and shea-butter-forward formula especially comforting on the skin. It should be noted that this formula includes artificial perfume, so fragrance-averse individuals should steer clear. But for those of us who want a special scent, a flake-free beard, and soothed skin, Blind Barber's beard oil does it all.

While I'd use most of the above options as both a hair oil and a beard oil, Aesop's is one where I think of it as a hair oil first and foremost. It brings control without making things look greasy, while trapping moisture and stopping frizz. I'll use it in short hair to tame down the sides, in medium lengths (mixed with a cream or clay) for added shine, or in long hair to prevent split ends. Then, once my hair's settled up, I'll run my hands through my beard afterward. So, if you want a great hair oil with beard benefits, Aesop's is the winner.

Since the beginning of the men's grooming boom, I've been waiting for the big designer fashion houses to start catering to guys with facial hair. For now, Tom Ford's beard oil stands alone. So, how does the designer oil stack up against our everyday favorites? After trying it out, I can tell you it’s better as a fragrance than a beard oil, but the scent alone earns it a spot in this guide.

The tobacco vanilla fragrance is much more sophisticated than what we’re used to seeing, or smelling, in this space. The scent puts an emphasis on vanilla, and you just need one or two pumps for full coverage. Considering the price and the name on the bottle, we were shocked to find this oil comes in a plastic pump bottle, but that fragrance. If you want to buy beard oil as a gift, this premium conditioning oil is a step up over your average Amazon brand, even if it doesn't soften coarse hair as well as some of our other options.

It has been revealed that if you have sensitive skin—or if you're afraid of your beard oil clashing with your daily cologne—then Marlowe makes one of the only fragrance-free beard oils. Most beard oil formulas contain both essential oils and some type of perfume oil (or, parfum, for my fellow ingredients detectives), which can be risky for your skin, follicles, and pores, so it’s nice to have an option for acne-prone and sensitive skin types.

This beard oil couldn’t be simpler—and I mean that in a good way. Marlowe No. 143 has an all-oil formula and just four ingredients: safflower seed oil, sunflower seed oil, corn oil, and soybean oil. That’s it. Considering the average beauty product contains up to a dozen ingredients we can’t even pronounce, it’s a refreshing change. Although, I have to say, if you want the softest possible beard, Honest Amish also makes a fragrance-free oil.

Most guys use beard oil to tame flyaways. But what if you want the thickest, fullest beard possible? In that case, I’d recommend reaching for Bevel’s oil. This brand makes skin and hair products for Black men, but anyone with coarse or curly hair can benefit from their products. GQ contributor Timothy Beck Werth reports that this oil gave him a thicker-looking beard without excess frizz, which isn't easy to do. (BTW, that’s as much as you can expect from any beard oil, so please don’t fall for the “beard growth serums” you’ll find all over the internet.).

For parched facial hair, the grapeseed, macadamia, jojoba, and argan oil will condition your beard and add a healthy shine. For beneath the scruff, the avocado and primrose oil with soothe your skin without clogging up your pores and follicles. Werth indicates this beard oil instantly softened his facial hair, and he also liked the sweeter smell of the macadamia-based formula. Most beard oils opt for woodsy fragrances, and the more subtle scent profile here is a nice surprise, he explains.

Sources indicate that anthony’s conditioning beard oil is a 2-in-1 product—a pre-shave oil and regular beard oil. That approach can be risky, since a lot of multipurpose products try to be everything and succeed at nothing, but luckily that’s not the case here. If you regularly cycle between clean-shaven, stubble, and full-on lighthouse keeper, then you can still use this product daily. As a pre-shave oil, it moisturizes the skin and softens facial hair for a smoother shave with fewer morning-after red bumps. As a beard oil, it hydrates, then locks in that moisture so your beard stays soft and shiny all day. I found the consistency to be somewhere in between a leave-in conditioner gel and a traditional oil, making it thicker and less messy to apply.

In a recent development, the oil also has an herbaceous, minty fragrance that’s so refreshing it feels like aromatherapy every time you run it through your hair. That’s because the formula is full of ingredients that smell good, feel good, and actually help your skin and hair. It uses carrier oils like soybean and castor to deliver skin-pleasing and antimicrobial botanicals such as rosemary, basil, tea tree oil, eucalyptus, and spearmint. And on the hydration front, calendula and olive oil nourish your whiskers into their softest, fluffiest selves. Because of the more complex fragrance and ingredients profile, this wouldn’t be my pick for guys with sensitive skin. Still, it’s a multi-functional serum you’ll look forward to using every day.

It has been revealed that lots of beard oils promise to get flyaways under control, yet those rogue hairs keep popping up. So, what do you do? Instead of trying yet another oil, try reaching for a product that’s more of a leave-in conditioner for your beard. We’ve previously praised Zeus’s beard brushes, but the California-based brand also makes a beard serum that deserves a spot in your bathroom cabinet. I love that this beard oil has the simplest possible ingredients list: sweet almond oil, soybean oil, argan seed oil, trihydroxystearin, avocado oil, and fragrance.

The only multi-syllable ingredient there is a simple thickening agent, which gives this refined beard oil a gel-like consistency. That thicker formula will also put flyaways in their place. The very subtle fragrance is more Mediterranean than winter pine forest (we tested the Verbena Lime version), but you can also opt for a fragrance-free formula if you have sensitive skin or allergies. The plastic bottle uses an air pump, letting you get every last drop of oil. For clean freaks who hate the messiness and spillage that always comes with beard oil application, this is another bonus.

Tired of being left out of couple’s skincare night just because those stupid sheet masks won’t hold onto your glorious beard? Cardon’s got you, boo. Actually, this bead oil hack is perfect for guys who only sparingly use beard oil on an as-needed basis.

Sources indicate that the bamboo and charcoal sheet mask is specially shaped for guys with beards, and each mask comes with a dose of beard oil made with argan and jojoba oil. In the Venn diagram of Korean skincare and beard care products, this sheet mask-beard oil duo is the tiny, microscopic bit of overlap in the middle.

Recent findings suggest that the best best oil should support your skin and your beard, and Baxter of California's sweet-smelling oil doesn't sacrifice one for the other. In his guide to the best beard care products, GQ's Timothy Beck Werth said that “In our testing, no beard oil absorbs as swiftly or spreads as evenly as this one.” Squalane helps nourish the most overlooked skin on your face, while avocado oil, vitamin E, and botanical extracts smooth out your beard.

Industry observers note that as with anything you put on your skin, the ingredients are what matter most. And with beard oils, there are two categories of ingredients: carrier oils and essential oils. No two ingredients will perform exactly the same. Some will help with very specific situations or conditions; some may actively aggravate your skin. Essential oils in particular can aggravate skin if used by themselves. So, consider the following carrier oils and essential oils, favored both by myself and Alyssa Bachowski, a senior barber at Fellow Barber’s Williamsburg, NYC barbershop.

According to recent reports, carrier oils—often vegetable and see oils—make up the bulk of these beard oil formulas, bringing beard nourishment and skin hydration. The most popular carrier oils are argan oil and jojoba oil (both of which Bachowski recommends), though there are dozens of varieties, from castor to marula to grape seed oils. They're usually unscented, though some—like coconut oil—may carry an aroma. Because carrier oils make up the “base” of the oil, they should be among the first to appear in a product's formula or list of ingredients.

“Jojoba oil is non-comedogenic, which means it will not clog your pores. It is also a lighter oil that is absorbent, so it won't just sit on top of the hair and give you a greasy appearance,” Bachowski notes. Along with argan oil, you’re going to see a lot of jojoba oil in most popular beard oil blends.

Sources indicate that “Argan oil is filled with a ton of vitamins and minerals, as well as linoleic acid, sterolins, and squalene. All of these aid in protecting and keeping your skin and beard healthy,” Bachowski claims.

“Castor oil is known for promoting beard hair growth,” claims Bachowski. It’s hypothetically the best beard-growth oil of the crew, because it acts like a vitamin for your strands—though there's more on that below in the FAQs. But don't expect it to grow more hairs, or thicker hairs. Castor oil does have a smoke-and-mirrors benefit, at least. “It is a heavier oil and dark in color, so it can give the appearance of a denser beard on men with dark facial hair,” Bachowski says.

Grape seed oil can help tone down your skin's oil production, and is extremely moisturizing for scruff and skin alike.

Rich in fatty acids, this is a frontrunner for “most nourishing oil” for your skin and whiskers.

Yes, shea butter is in fact a carrier oil, and it has supremely moisturizing properties that make it great for detangling scraggly beards and softening stiff hairs.

Essential oils are distillations from more potent sources, and they tend to be additive—and active—ingredients in a beard oil. These oils are typically extracted through steaming methods, and their range of benefits can include antimicrobial properties, oil-toning abilities, and soothing superpowers. Typically, any natural fragrance in a beard oil will come from essential oils. But pure essential oils can be extremely damaging to the skin.

“You should not apply pure essential oil to a beard—it will do the opposite of what you are trying to achieve,” Bachowski says. “These [pure oils] are not good for your beard nor your skin. as they can be irritating and harmful. Essential oils can cause dryness, itchiness, and redness—and some people may have allergic reactions to them.” This is exactly why you want beard oils from trusted, tested brand.

Sources indicate that bachowski likes cedarwood oil for its naturally astringent properties. “It helps cleanse the pores and prevent ingrown hairs,” she adds. It also adds a natural fragrance.

“Sandalwood has anti-inflammatory properties that help reduce any skin irritation,” Bachowski says of this deliciously scented oil.

It has been revealed that lavender helps calm inflammation and redness, says Bachowski. Plus it brings lavender's soothing scent.

This antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, oil-toning ingredient is terrific for acne-prone faces and oily skin types.

Along with its refreshing scent, grapefruit peel oil helps nourish and detangle.

According to recent reports, as GQ's lead grooming product reviewer, I've tried just about every beard oil in the biz. The ones chosen for this roundup excel at protecting and moisturizing both skin and hair, with minimal risk for things like inverse reactions and blemishes. They absorb cleanly, unless they expressly choose not to (like those which expressly use silicone), and they smell terrific (with both natural and artificially scented options). I've tested beard oils for a decade, on a beard that's been long, short, and everything in between. I've also scoured online reviews to confirm that these products are backed by throngs of loyal fans, whose collective opinion echoes my own experiences.

What is the best beard oil according to GQ?

Recent findings suggest that with more than a decade of testing beard oils under his belt, GQ’s expert tester chose Honest Amish as the best beard oil. And 29,000 Amazon shoppers have rated this same product 4.5 out of 5 stars.

In a recent development, what is the difference between beard balm vs. oil?

In a recent development, both beard balm and beard oil are both terrific for facial hair—but they don't do the same job. Beard balm is optimal for taming and styling facial hair, especially at medium and longer lengths. Beard oil provides less control over the shape and style, but is excellent at softening and conditioning the hairs and the skin underneath (preventing beard itch, beard dandruff, and split ends).

After using a beard wash, most beard oils are applied the same way: “Start off with 2-3 drops in the palm of your hand,” claims Bachowski. “Rub it into your hands so that it is evenly distributed from fingertips to the heel of your hand. Start by rubbing the oil with your fingertips onto the skin beneath the beard hair, then eventually working the oil from root to tip of the actual beard. Make sure to also apply oil to your neck and cheeks where you may have shaved or trimmed as well. If you feel like the 2-3 drops wasn't enough based on the length or density of your beard, apply another 2-3 drops.”.

How do you prevent beard dandruff?

Recent findings suggest that preventing beard dandruff starts with changing your skincare regimen. Namely, introducing exfoliation and moisturizing products that can get past a thick nest of facial hair. For exfoliation, look for physical scrubs (even a beard brush will work). For the best moisturizing effects, be sure to apply beard oil both morning and night. The beard oil will also soften and condition the facial hair to prevent itchiness.

Does beard oil help grow a beard?

Industry observers note that no, beard oil is not meant to help beard hair growth, whether that’s to make facial hair thicker or grow faster. To be honest, we don’t know of much that can really change your scruff's density besides a beard transplant and maybe minoxidil. Beard oil is here to make your existing beard hair softer and more cooperative, while also nourishing the skin beneath the beard—skin that’s often prone to dehydration and dandruff. It’s already doing a lot.

Industry observers note that absolutely. Beard oil is a great investment for anyone with facial hair, since it can help soften and tame your scruff while simultaneously moisturizing the skin underneath. This means no more itching, no flyaways, and no beard dandruff.

Alyssa Bachowski is a senior barber at Fellow Barber’s Williamsburg NYC barbershop location.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

According to recent reports, note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, promptly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

It has been revealed that to a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

It has been revealed that scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

Recent findings suggest that there are two sorts of Parisian holidays. The first, an exercise in blissful escapism, where luxury hotels, gallery hopping, and lazy apéros à la terrasse all help you lean into the romantic undercurrent of the city. The second, an exercise in make-believe: You would not be the first person to plot a move to Paris halfway through your stay there, earmarking local boulangeries and wine shops as favorites and spending mornings chit-chatting with market vendors. If you lean toward the latter experience, this is where the best Airbnbs in Paris enter the picture. After all, what better way to cosplay a Parisienne than via a cozy flat of your own (albeit a temporary one)?

Recent findings suggest that our edit is an evolving one—there’s no shortage of stately Haussmann buildings available for rent—grouped by arrondissement. (There are 20 total, and while we haven’t hit on all of them, the below list includes several of the most popular for visitors.) Each spot has its own distinct flair, depending on what sort of Parisian you wish to embody. The chichi traveler with high-brow tastes will love the classic charm of the Left Bank; the arty fashion-lover will prefer the cozy studios of the Marais (as well as its proximity to some of the best vintage shops); the low-key bohemian will find respite in the hills of Montmarte, above the city’s lights. Grand architecture and bistro balconies, you’ll be glad to discover, have no loyalty to any particular arrondissement. They’re all good; you really can’t go wrong.

For anyone planning a trip to the City of Light, consider the roundup of properties ahead for a true immersive experience in one of the most stylish cities on the planet.

According to recent reports, for a grand apartment right in the middle of the historical center, book this ornate Airbnb. Travelers looking to see all the sights will appreciate its proximity to the Palais Royal, Centre Pompidou, and the Louvre; it’s also around the corner from the Les Halles shopping center, where you’ll find both great restaurants (Le Petit Bouillon Pharamond is a nice option for an affordable lunch and gorgeous interiors) and little shops (E. Dehillerin, Julia Child’s much-frequented kitchenware store, is a must). The home itself is no less impressive—high ceilings with crown molding, antique gilded mirrors, and parquet floors run throughout.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, indoor fireplace, long-term stays allowed, elevator.

Sources indicate that exposed beams and parquet flooring set the scene for this typically charming Parisian apartment. There’s lots of space for making yourself right at home, including a stunning balcony that sits atop Rue de Rivoli so you’ll feel like you’re right in the middle of everything as you sip your morning espresso while mapping out the day’s itinerary. Then there’s the location: If it’s your first time visiting Paris, the fact that the Louvre museum, the Centre Pompidou, and the Seine are all within walking distance will be a massive bonus. Leave the complicated commutes for your sophomore outing; this home lets you walk everywhere.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, blackout shades, Devialet Bluetooth sound system, television, air conditioning, kitchen, dishwasher, espresso machine, balcony, housekeeping available at a cost.

Best for: First-timers to the city.

This sun-drenched two-bedroom near the Seine opens with a grand, golden-colored lobby, complete with a spiral staircase and tile floors. Upstairs, the duplex has lots of space to stretch out, from a dining table that doubles as a workspace to a bright living room to a small balcony. You’ll have both the fifth and sixth floors—but as there’s no elevator, prepare to get your cardio in. It’s in a fun area, too; Pizzeria Popolare, a great Italian restaurant, is just down the street, and you’re within easy exploring distance of all the boutiques and galleries the Marais has to offer.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, Bluetooth sound system, television, balcony, pets allowed.

Best for: A small group of friends—who still want their own space.

According to recent reports, we’d book this Airbnb for the tiles alone. From the rainbow-colored bathtub to the celery green kitchen to the traditional tomettes that run throughout, it’s an effortlessly charming spot, located on the third floor of an 18th-century building. The enviable design continues from the baby blue bedroom to the painted furniture; it’ll be more than obvious that you’re staying in one of the more creative, artistic quartiers of the city. (And if you want to get some of your own work done, the dedicated office area is happy to oblige.) While it’s in a bustling neighborhood, the apartment itself is at the back of the property, so you’ll have quiet when you need it.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 3.

Amenities: Bathtub, elevator, coffee maker, building staff.

If you picked the Marais because of its art scene, you might as well commit to the experience and book an Airbnb directly overlooking the Picasso Museum. Sought-after location aside, this duplex feels welcoming from the moment you step in the door. Hexagonal terracotta tiles line the floor, a large dining table is the perfect spot for a cozy night in, and every nook and cranny is filled with glass vases and art. When you want to head out for dinner, you’re spoilt for choice—but start with Chez Nenesse, a classic, red-and-white checkered tablecloth bistrot, that’s just four minutes away.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Kitchen, washer, Bose sound system, indoor fireplace, coffee maker.

The first thing this Airbnb has going for it is its location: It’s situated right on the Île Saint-Louis, one of the city’s two islands, and therefore has a more quaint feel to it than some of the busier arrondissements. (Plus you’re just five minutes from Berthillon, the best ice cream in the area.) The second thing, of course, is its style. The building itself is listed as a historic monument dating back to the 17th century, and interior highlights like a painted ceiling and gilded mirror amplify the antique appeal. Even the piano area, a tiny nook off one of the bedrooms, has a blue marble floor and matching tile mural—it’s all extremely decadent.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 6.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, piano, indoor fireplace, parking, hot tub.

Sources indicate that we found your Parisian tree house. Tucked away near the busy Place des Vosges, the fourth-floor apartment is a calm respite, well-sized for a couple or solo traveler in search of more unique accommodation. Here, rustic wood beams accent nearly every ceiling and wall, textured brick flooring adds warmth, and a large, tiled tub looks out onto Haussmannian rooftops for a truly cozy stay. It even has two balconies—sure, they may be tiny, but the sweeping views of the city’s architecture more than makes up for their size.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 3.

Amenities: Washer, television, piano, balcony, bathtub.

Best for: Those looking for a non-traditional vacation rental.

A bedroom adorned in pink toile de Jouy print, a working fireplace in the living room, a dining room that’s overflowing with plants and dressed up with a gilded mirror: this apartment, to borrow some first-level French, is très chic. It’s deceptively spacious—thanks to a sofa bed, it can actually sleep up to six people—making it ideal for a girls’ trip to the city. With a spacious living area and a well-equipped kitchen, it’s certainly designed to handle a larger group. A nice bonus? You’re within walking distance of the beloved bookstore Shakespeare and Company for a souvenir you can employ on the long flight home.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroom; sleeps 6.

Amenities: Kitchen, TV, fireplace, washer/dryer, bathtub.

Steps away from the bustling Odéon neighborhood and landmarks like the Pantheon and the Luxembourg Garden, this apartment is ideally situated for first-timers to the city of lights. With original 1930s features preserved and played up, it's also well-decorated: Art Deco details, like geometric borders, curved ceiling cut-outs, and arched doorways pop up throughout. (The turquoise bathtub nook is a particular highlight; the glass wall in the dining room is another.) This rental has tons of space for a family as well as several kid-friendly amenities available upon request; book it for a longer stay in the city.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 6.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, piano, Bluetooth sound system, exercise equipment, television, high chair, board games, elevator, parking, pets allowed.

Location: By the Pantheon and the Luxembourg Garden.

Best for: Art Deco aficionados.

This literary, light-filled Airbnb is located in a building that houses several artists studios—notes of which can be found everywhere from the airy, industrial-style layout to the perfectly imperfect collection of decor to the multi-colored tiles in the kitchen. (As for the literary tie-in: Bookworms will appreciate the massive wall of books in the upstairs bedroom. Take your pick.) The home is mere blocks away from the Jardin du Luxembourg, in Montparnasse. Browse the aforementioned bookshelf and grab a paperback, pick up a coffee from one of the many cafés in the area, and take a morning to yourself in the gardens.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Kitchen, washer/dryer, TV, crib, courtyard.

Location: Near Jardin du Luxembourg.

Best for: Avid readers always looking for a fresh, picturesque spot to get lost in a book.

In a recent development, for the solo traveler who never wants to be too far from the sparkling lights of the Eiffel Tower, this little studio is a cozy cocoon just six minutes away. (Starting quite literally with the bed, which is cordoned off from the rest of the space by a chic glass wall and a gauzey curtain.) A tiny kitchenette stocked with all the essential appliances lets you make the most of local treats—helpful, as the famous Rue Cler street market is just around the corner, so you can stock up on cheeses, quiche, and even rotisserie chickens for quiet meals at home.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 3.

Amenities: Washer, elevator, pet-friendly, housekeeping available at a fee.

Location: On Rue Amélie, a quick walk to the Eiffel Tower.

Best for: Foodies traveling alone.

Sources indicate that it’ll be hard to beat this central location: This sunny, spacious two-bedroom is situated directly at the base of the Champ de Mars, the grassy park that houses the Eiffel Tower. It’s as stately as its zip code implies—think, period-appropriate wall moldings that reflect its 19th-century origins and oversized windows, with the occasional unexpected pop of color (like a yellow window in the kitchen and pistachio dining chairs) to keep it from feeling stuffy. It also comes with an espresso machine, so if you ever tire of your local boulangerie—unlikely—you can start the day with coffee at home.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 3.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, elevator.

Location: At the foot of the Eiffel Tower.

Best for: Ticking the Eiffel Tower off your bucket list.

It’s conveniently located in the heart of Paris and stocked with modern creature comforts like a Nespresso machine and a Netflix-enabled television, but you really only need one reason to book this apartment: the massive terrace. Equipped with outdoor dining and seating, it’s a rare thing to find in the busy city (and, should you ever want a little quiet, an ideal spot to enjoy an apéro at home). Though it only has one proper bedroom, it can actually sleep four thanks to a sofa bed in the living room. For families looking for a comfortable spot near all the top sights, this is a great option.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Washer, blackout shades, HDTV, Bose sound system, exercise equipment, travel crib, kitchen, Nespresso coffee maker, dishwasher, terrace, paid parking available.

Location: In the Champs-Elysées area.

Best for: Travelers for whom a terrace with a view is a non-negotiable.

Recent findings suggest that staying in this palatial sixth-floor penthouse will feel like time travel—it sits within a historic Haussmann building and offers original details like 18th-century wood floors, hand-painted wallpaper, antique fireplaces, and a Napoleon-style oval room. It’s bourgeois luxury in every sense. The entire space enjoys plenty of light thanks to French windows opening onto three balconies, and amenities like a full kitchen and entry hall with a piano will make it difficult to venture outside (though you’ll want to—it’s in close proximity to some of Paris’s most coveted attractions like the Louvre, Opera Garnier, Champs Élysées).

Rooms: 4 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 8.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, piano, kitchen, elevator, balcony, antique fireplaces.

Location: In the Champs Elysées district.

Best for: Anyone who knows what a “Napoleon-style oval room” is (interior design buffs, this one’s for you).

On the fifth floor of a traditional Haussmann building (there is an elevator, don’t worry) sits this elegant sunny spot. A long balcony stretches outside and includes a small bistro set for breakfasts outside—though the spacious dining room is also an enticing option. From the red-and-cream checkerboard kitchen to the ornate crown molding in the living area, it’s endlessly charming. Montmartre is only 15 minutes away; perhaps more importantly, depending on what your itinerary priorities are, the famous bakery Mamiche is an even-shorter 10 minute walk. (The brioche and the ham sandwich alone are good reasons to make a daily pilgrimage there each morning.).

Rooms: 4 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 5.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, sound system, board games, fire place, balcony, elevator.

Best for: Design inspiration and proximity to an incredible bakery.

Originally belonging to the painter Georges Braque back in 1911, this sweet studio has since been re-done and can now fit up to four guests (the sofa converts to a bed, if you don’t mind a slightly crowded living space). The renovation didn’t strip it of its character, though, and between the primary-colored kitchen storage cubbies and the floor-to-ceiling windows that let the light stream in, it’s one of the more unique apartment rentals in Paris. The bay windows look out onto a courtyard, so you’ll have plenty of peace despite being located in one of the city’s most bustling areas for nightlife.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, kitchen, shared backyard, coffee maker, crib/travel crib/children’s books available upon request, balcony.

Location: In the Pigalle neighborhood.

Best for: Those hoping to experience the city’s artistic spirit beyond a visit to the Louvre.

Right below Pigalle on Rue Cadet, this quiet one-bedroom is surrounded by bakeries, cheese shops, and greengrocers. Everything you’d need is within walking distance; head to Racines, a hole-in-the-wall Italian spot with a decadent tiramisù, for a date night in the neighborhood. Inside, a fully equipped kitchen and multiple workspaces ensure you have all the essentials to stretch out and make this temporary spot feel like home. With sloping ceilings and views onto the city’s greyscale rooftops, it feels like the coziest attic—peaceful, personal, and chic enough to make you want to stay awhile.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Washer, kitchen, dishwasher, coffee maker.

Location: In the Grand Boulevards area.

Best for: A cozy couples getaway.

Industry observers note that if you can’t pick between the trendy 10th or 3rd arrondissements—don’t. This bright and airy one-bedroom is smack in the middle, in an ideal area full of hole-in-the-wall eateries and stylish spots to grab an apéro before a late dinner. Since it’s owned and designed by an architect, its interiors are especially appealing: The blend of vintage furniture and flourishing greenery might just inspire you to redecorate when you get home. In the meantime, you’ll feel right at home. The kitchen is big enough to whip up meals of your own, if you feel inspired—or at least, a quick breakfast before heading out for the day.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, blackout shades, HDTV, Apple sound system, piano, kitchen, dishwasher, Nespresso coffee maker.

Location: Right on the border of the 10th and the 3rd arrondissements.

Best for: Bookmarking design inspiration.

Overlooking the rooftops of Paris, this small but well-appointed apartment (yes, it has an elevator) is perfect for a couple. From a zellige-tiled kitchen to a teeny balcony where you can sip a cocktail during golden hour, you’ll find everything you need for a short stint in the city. But the best part is, hands down, its location: The home is right by the Canal. Here, you’ll find a livelier, younger scene, with natural wine bars, trendy restaurants, and an atmosphere that feels decidedly removed from the touristy center. (Early June, a local-favorite restaurant and wine bar with a rotating cast of guest chefs, is a leisurely 15-minute walk away.).

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Washer, balcony, kitchen.

Location: Near the Canal St. Martin.

Best for: Proximity to your fresh favorite wine bar.

For a vacation rental that feels designed by someone’s French grandma, choose this colorful, eclectic spot and make yourself at home. The kitchen, with its checkerboard-covered table, citron walls, and collected jumble of various tools and trinkets, is undoubtedly the center; but the bedrooms (there are three), with their massive windows and original terracotta floors are also nice—especially if you’re traveling with a significant group, and want to make sure you each have enough space. When you do want to dine out, you’ll be well-positioned: Bistrot des Tournelles and Chez Paul, two wonderful traditional bistros, are located in this neighborhood.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 5.

Best for: Cosplaying Julia Child for the weekend.

According to recent reports, not all Parisian Airbnbs involve ornate crown moldings and baroque antiques; some, like this loft, can lean quite industrial. Iron beams and high ceilings make it seem even more spacious (the space itself is located in an old printing house); glass windows overlook an internal courtyard, if you need a quiet temporary home. Sandwiched between République and Canal St. Martin, it’s in a fun, more local part of the city. If it’s warm enough, walk along the water in the afternoon before ducking into Chambre Noir, a little wine bar near the apartment, for small plates and a crisp glass of white.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, TV, air conditioning, pet-friendly.

Best for: Fans of industrial architecture.

Sources indicate that this two-bedroom apartment may just house the best balcony in all of Paris. It’s well-furnished, with plenty of potted plants and a bistro set for taking your breakfast outside, weather-permitting, but the views of the Haussmann buildings and Eiffel Tower in the distance are what makes it really special. Inside, the design is cozy, with floral quilts and Art Deco-inspired lighting casting everything in a warm glow. Even the entrance to the apartment is special. While the fifth floor rental is accessible by elevator, you may just find yourself choosing to take the stairs, which are lined with stained glass windows.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, Sonos Bluetooth sound system, indoor fireplace, air conditioning, coffee maker, balcony, outdoor furniture, elevator.

Best for: Morning coffee on the balcony.

Perched in the heart of Montmartre in the hilly, cobblestone-lined streets of the Abbesses neighborhood, this one-bedroom home is ideal for the couple who likes their decor collected, full of personality, and a tiny bit mismatched. Starting with the mix of antique furnishings in the living room (including a red velvet armchair) and going right through to the lemon-yellow bedroom, the design of this place will make you feel like you’re visiting your artistic Parisian friend—no cold, white-box rooms here. When you do want to hit the tourist spots, the Basilica of Sacré Coeur is just a 15-minute walk away.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Best for: The eclectic traveler coming to Paris to peruse the flea markets.

Industry observers note that you’re alone in Paris, and you need an inspiring studio from which to focus on your creative project (or just finish your book in peace): This artist’s loft is it. Tall ceilings and an oversized window create a light-filled environment, while a dedicated workspace offers a quiet place to concentrate. There’s a small but well-appointed kitchen so you can cook your meals at home and truly feel at ease during your stay, however long it may be.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Washer, crib, coffee maker, shared backyard.

Best for: Anyone coming to Paris to get out of a creative rut.

From the terracotta tomettes to the oversized windows, this sunny one-bedroom is perfect for the solo traveler or a couple. The building dates back to the 19th century, but the decor is firmly 21st: Butter yellow bedding and a mustard-striped kitchen skirt are design ideas to bookmark for when you get home. And you can’t trump the location: It’s right in the heart of Montmartre, only a few blocks away from Boulangerie Raphaëlle (one of the all-time best bakeries in the city—trust us).

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Travel crib available upon request, coffee maker.

Best for: An extended solo trip.

Jeans and ballerinas are the unofficial uniform of the city (and, conveniently, make a comfortable ensemble for a day of shopping). Bring an extra-large tote as your personal item on the plane so you have plenty of space to shuttle back all your souvenirs… including some French pharmacy goodies, of course.

According to recent reports, after combing through hundreds of listings in a destination’s most desirable neighborhoods, we narrow down our list by reviewing a variety of determining factors, from the logistics of price, location, and amenities, to important details such as reviews and host information. From there, we take into consideration aesthetic details such as design, natural light, and overall look and feel of the home. The final edit is a well-rounded list that ensures booking a stay will result in a safe and stylish holiday.

Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando’s Complete Relationship Timeline

📅 19 Nov 2024 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Miley Cyrus can buy herself flowers, but we have a feeling that her beau, Maxx Morando, is buying them for her.
  • Since 2021, the Disney Channel alum has been linked to Morando, a fellow musician who is perhaps best known as being the drummer for the rock band Liily.
  • Throughout their years-long relationship, the two have preferred to keep their romance largely out of the spotlight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Miley Cyrus can buy herself flowers, but we have a feeling that her beau, Maxx Morando, is buying them for her.

Since 2021, the Disney Channel alum has been linked to Morando, a fellow musician who is perhaps best known as being the drummer for the rock band Liily. He was also previously part of another group, called the Regrettes. In 2022, Lilly was invited to play on Cyrus’s TV special, Miley’s Newly introduced Year’s Eve Party.

Throughout their years-long relationship, the two have preferred to keep their romance largely out of the spotlight. But Cyrus offered a rare glimpse into their life together during her interview for the Harper’s Bazaar’s December 2024/January 2025 cover story. “He’s very similar to me,” she mentioned. “We just don’t take life too seriously.”.

According to recent reports, throughout their time together, they’ve also collaborated numerous times in the studio, with Morando serving as a producer and songwriter on Cyrus’s Something Beautiful and Bass Persuades records. In her interview with Bazaar, Cyrus revealed that music was actually how she and Morando first got to know each other. “I’ve always worked with the people that I love,” Cyrus said. “And Maxx just inspires me so much.”.

According to recent reports, now, the pair are engaged and reported to be getting married this weekend with an intimate ceremony in Southern California. However, other details are being kept under wraps—for now.

If you’re wondering what else there is to know about Cyrus and Morando’s low-key romance, then look no further. Below, we’ve tracked the couple’s entire relationship from start to finish.

For Cyrus, it was love at first sight, but for Morando, he already had an idea of who he was meeting long before the date even happened.

In a recent development, “We got put on a blind date,” Cyrus reveals in an interview with British Vogue years after the fact, in May 2023. “Well, it was blind for me and not really for him. I thought, ‘The worst that can happen is I leave.’ ”.

When he calls mid-interview, her phone starts playing “Tyrone” by Erykah Badu. “I call that ‘boyfriend sexy ringtone,’ ” she claims, smiling.

In an interview with Vogue, Cyrus discusses the outfits that she wore for her sets at Summerfest in Milwaukee and Atlanta’s Music Midtown festival. Turns out, one of the pieces—a faux-leather set crafted by Shane Kastl—includes cartoon monsters sketched by Morando.

According to recent reports, during the interview, Cyrus comments on the custom design, saying, “This look is a one-of-a-kind collaboration between two of my favorite emerging artists, Maxx Morando and Shane Kastl. Shane used existing pieces I’ve collected over time and customized Maxx’s cartoon characters [within] his construction. Their collaboration is the perfect example of sustainability becoming the next fashion phase, and it proves that anything can be reinvented, which resonates with me deeply.”.

The pair spark dating rumors when they make their first public appearance at the Gucci Love Parade fashion show in November.

It has been revealed that for the event, Cyrus wears a metallic blue fringe dress with a contrasting cream feather drop waist, which she pairs with strappy golden sandals. Meanwhile, Morando sports a burgundy suit over a G-logo top, with white sneakers featuring the signature Gucci red and green stripes.

Shortly after the event, Cyrus shares a slideshow where the third photo sees her and Morando posing together on the red carpet. In her caption, the singer writes, “LOVE PARADE ❤️💕 @gucci @alessandro_michele.”.

A fan captures a sweet video of Morando supporting Cyrus backstage for her NBC holiday special, Miley’s New Year’s Eve Party. In the clip, the two can be seen smiling and dancing together.

Days later, paparazzi snap photos of the two enjoying a vacation together in Miami, where the special was filmed.

Cyrus and Morando make a rare joint appearance together for Versace’s Fall/Winter 2023 fashion show in West Hollywood.

It has been revealed that later in the day, the two attend the launch party for Cyrus’s eighth studio album, Endless Summer Vacation, in Beverly Hills. Paparazzi photos—which you can see here—show Cyrus dressed to the nines in a sparkly black one-shoulder minidress and a vibrant green fur jacket. Morando looks equally stylish in a navy-blue velvet suit.

A source tells People where Cyrus’s head is at amid her relationship with Morando.

“She’s the healthiest and happiest she’s been in a long time,” the source says, then goes on to describe how Cyrus has healed following her 2020 divorce from Liam Hemsworth: “Everyone was blaming her for the divorce and calling her this wild child, but that wasn’t fair. Their relationship and marriage was toxic, and she was heartbroken.”.

A second insider tells the outlet that Morando is a “cool guy.”.

Recent findings suggest that “He has no interest in being a huge celebrity; he’s very low-key. Miley loves these qualities,” the source explains. “Miley can be herself. They are supportive of each other’s careers. Miley is enjoying life and things are great.”.

Morando supports Cyrus at the 66th-annual Grammy Awards ceremony, where the singer wins her first-ever golden gramophone.

During the ceremony, the couple is joined by Cyrus’s family members, mom Tish Cyrus and sister Brandi Cyrus.

A source for People opens up about Cyrus and Morando’s joyful home life together.

“She is very happy with him,” the insider claims. “Miley has changed a lot in the past couple of years. She seems more calm and harmonious. Everyone loves Maxx. He’s a great guy. She is very happy with him. He’s private and doesn’t like being in the press. It’s been good for her.”.

In a newly introduced Dolce & Gabbana campaign video, Cyrus poses in a sultry all-black look and shares the song “Imitate,” a track from Morando’s band, Liily.

Cyrus offers rare details on her love story with Morando in an interview for Bazaar’s December 2024/January 2025 cover story.

It has been revealed that “He’s very similar to me. We just don’t take life too seriously,” she says.

While the two have a small age gap—Cyrus is six years Morando’s senior—she reflects on how their different upbringings have made them approach life differently.

“He looks at life really differently than I do,” she explains. “He grew up with a laptop. I had a desktop computer that I shared with my brothers and sisters. … Honestly, he’s raised our dog off Reddit. I’m like, Are you sure we’re supposed to be doing this? And he’s like, On Reddit it claims blah, blah, blah.”.

She also opens up about working with Morando on musical projects and how collaboration is her love language. “I worked with my dad forever. That’s how me and my ex-husband met each other. I’ve always worked with the people that I love,” Cyrus says. “And Maxx just inspires me so much.”.

Morando and Cyrus are photographed behind-the-scenes at the 67th Grammy Awards, where Cyrus snags her third Grammy for her collaboration on Beyoncé’s “II Most Wanted.” The appearance marks a rare joint public outing by the couple, who match in all-black ensembles.

Morando wears his usual red-carpet uniform to stand by his partner at the 97th Academy Awards. Cyrus wears a black gown with a distressed bodice embellished with sequins, which she wears with a curly hairdo and bleached brows.

Cyrus and Morando walk the red carpet for the Hollywood premiere of Avatar: Fire and Ash, and there, the singer debuts a chunky gold ring with a large, square diamond at the center.

Hours later, People confirms the two are engaged.

The engaged pair wear cool all-black looks to the show and look so in love as they embrace at their star-studded table during the ceremony.

💡 Key Takeaways

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Spoilers below for The Hunger Games books, including Sunrise on the Reaping.

Re-reading the original The Hunger Games series in preparation for this review, I started experiencing nightmares. Despite my generally overactive imagination, I would not call this normal. I read a lot of fiction, much of it politically prescient if not outright dystopian; if everything I consumed brought on such sleep paralysis demons, I’d call a doctor. But I shouldn’t be surprised that, now, Suzanne Collins’s young-adult trilogy began seeping into my subconscious, 15 years after I’d first turned its final page—especially considering that it’s now the latest in her series to become a feature film.

In a recent development, the lead protagonist in Collins’s trilogy, Katniss Everdeen, spends the entire series battling such nightmares as the death toll escalates around her. After volunteering as a tribute in the Capitol’s annual Hunger Games, pitting children against each other in a fight to the death, her already difficult life in District 12 becomes outright dangerous. She inadvertently sparks a rebellion. She leads that rebellion. She loses countless loved ones. Those of us who read and adored the series know how it ends, but even those unfamiliar with Katniss’s struggle can take an educated guess. Protest rarely goes unpunished.

Recent findings suggest that I can’t claim to have experienced anywhere near the trauma Katniss undergoes throughout Collins’s trilogy, but I have aged considerably since I first read those books, and what struck me most as I re-encountered familiar passages was how present they still felt. I’d expected some nostalgia whilst leafing through The Hunger Games, Catching Fire, and Mockingjay, and the same when I’d pick up Collins’s latest installment in the franchise, the prequel novel Sunrise on the Reaping. I had not expected to feel so disturbed. Or so furious.

This is the crowning achievement of Sunrise on the Reaping, which succeeds in the near-impossible task of making an well-trodden story feel as intimate and visceral as its predecessors. Reaping is the fifth Hunger Games novel and the second prequel installment after The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which chronicled the youth and radicalization of the future president of Panem, Coriolanus Snow. (Like the original trilogy, Songbirds was adapted into a hugely popular Lionsgate film in 2023, and Reaping’s own adaptation landed in 2026.) Reaping surges forward a handful of years, set nearly a quarter of a century before Katniss’s own Hunger Games.

The story centers on Haymitch Abernathy, a beloved figure in The Hunger Games trilogy, in which he plays the role of the embittered if endearing drunk whose previous Hunger Games victory sets him up as mentor to Katniss and her District 12 partner, Peeta, for their own. In Reaping, Katniss and Peeta have yet to be born, but a young Haymitch knows their parents well. Here, Collins does a remarkable job of delivering what fans would call devastating “lore drops,” but she does so, for the most part, without resorting to cheesy or unnecessary Easter eggs. These minor characters—including Katniss’s parents, Burdock Everdeen and Asterid March—serve a clear purpose: to ground Haymitch in a familiar-but-reoriented District 12, where rebellion is yearned for but rarely acted upon.

One of the few characters willing to risk their wellbeing in pursuit of justice is Lenore Dove, Haymitch’s girlfriend and a descendant of the Covey, a group of former nomads whom readers will recognize from Songbirds. Her conviction, her music, and her love (“like all-fire,” she says, one of several Covey expressions employed throughout the book) steers Haymitch to her aid at the annual reaping ceremony, during which child tributes are selected for the Hunger Games. This year is a Quarter Quell, and the Capitol will demand twice as many boy and girl tributes as in an average year. After an unexpected execution takes place in the District 12 square, Haymitch finds himself rounded up with three other tributes and sent to spar for his life in the Gamemakers’ brutal arena.

Industry observers note that this is, of course, not a spoiler: Haymitch wins. Collins first described Haymitch’s victory way back in 2009 with the release of Catching Fire, during which Katniss and Peeta watch a recap video of Haymitch’s Quarter Quell. Through Katniss’s eyes, the young Haymitch comes off as “snarky. Arrogant. Indifferent.” But what Katniss doesn’t know is that the footage she’s watching has been heavily edited to reorder the timeline of events in the arena, and to remove Haymitch’s repeated efforts to undermine the Capitol. When he wins the games, he does so not as a ruthless survivor, but as a rebel attempting to break the arena itself. And when he returns home as a reluctant victor, he pays for his revolution a hundredfold.

Industry observers note that we already knew from Catching Fire that, mere weeks after the Quell, President Snow orders Haymitch’s mother, brother, and girlfriend to be killed. But it’s something else entirely to experience those deaths on the page. In Sunrise on the Reaping, this mother, brother, and girlfriend are no longer nameless extensions of Haymitch himself; they are characters we’ve come to know (named Willamae, Sid, and Lenore Dove), whose deaths we dread despite their inevitability. Our anticipation does not ultimately erase our pain, just as pre-grieving an ailing loved one does not ultimately erase their loss. Collins understands this well, and she uses our emotions to target our instincts for both ignorance and apathy.

In a recent development, in the end, Haymitch’s own assumed apathy cannot hold. He drives away his friends and few remaining neighbors, turning to “sleep syrup” and rotgut liquor as he’s tormented by violent memories and recurring echoes of “The Raven” by Edgar Allen Poe, which, in the world of Panem, has been passed down through the generations to become Lenore Dove’s “name poem.” In Poe’s famous 1845 poem, an unnamed narrator mourns the death of his lover, his “lost Lenore.” He is caught between two dueling desires: the temptation to forget Lenore and the desperation to remember her. His late-night visitor, a raven who only repeats the word “nevermore,” insists upon remembrance, driving the narrator to conclude that only madness awaits him.

Haymitch makes a similar conclusion—for the time being, anyway—as he wakes half-drunk from nightmares but stays alive, Lenore Dove’s final wish having “condemned [Haymitch] to life.” (She begs that he not let another sun rise on a reaping day, thus giving the book its title.) And though the word-for-word replication of “The Raven” in Sunrise on the Reaping is one of Collins’s few missteps—later eliminated by the movie adaptation—drawing the reader away from Haymitch’s world, the poem nevertheless carries a deeply poignant message.

Thematically, much of Sunrise on the Reaping is about propaganda, and specifically how truth is manipulated to trigger an audience’s emotional response. The Capitol Gamemakers edit footage of Haymitch to confirm what Capitol residents already want to believe about him—that he is a charming but ultimately dangerous rascal—and to ignore what does not suit their “logic.” As Plutarch Heavensbee (another character from the original trilogy) tells Haymitch and his allies, “People have an emotional response to something, then they come up with an argument for why it logically makes sense.” That explains the so-called “necessity” of the Hunger Games themselves: By convincing the Capitol residents to fear and deride the Districts, and the Districts to fear and covet the Capitol, the Capitol citizens are able to stomach the Hunger Games as “for the greater good”—and the Districts ultimately succumb to the resulting authoritarianism. History, as they say, is written by the victors.

But while propaganda is indeed a form of storytelling, there is a chasm of difference between twisting stories with malicious intent and preserving them for posterity. Collins’s use of “The Raven,” in addition to numerous other songs and poems popular amongst the Covey, is a testament to that fact. That a poem from 1845 would exist, in its entirety, numerous centuries in the future—having survived the collapse of North American society and the building of a totalitarian government bent on killing children—is something of a wondrous idea to behold. It is also a nod to the strength and resilience of the Covey themselves, who have taken care to maintain these stories despite the Capitol’s relentless and well-documented censorship.

Industry observers note that as in Mockingjay and Songbirds, Sunrise on the Reaping ends with an epilogue. This final chapter leaps decades into the future, taking place in the years after Mockingjay and its siege on the Capitol. When Katniss and Peeta choose to compile a post-war “memorial book,” Collins writes that Haymitch is not initially interested in contributing. “What use?” she writes, from his perspective. “What point? To relive all the loss. But when Burdock’s page came up, I had to mention him showing me [Lenore’s] grave. And I felt compelled to tell them about Maysilee Donner, former owner of the mockingjay pin. And how Sid loved the stars. Before I knew it, they all came tumbling out: family, tributes, friends, comrades in arms, everybody, even my love. I finally told our story.”.

According to recent reports, haymitch realizes that forgetting was never really an option. It wasn’t an option for the narrator of “The Raven,” nor is it an option for him. Choosing to forget would be capitulating to a system that manipulates such forgetfulness for power-hungry aims. Intentional amnesia, learned apathy—both would be an abdication of love.

15 years after Mockingjay was released, I needn’t wonder why the series brought on refreshed nightmares. Authoritarianism is not a fictional threat. It has not been dreamed up for our entertainment or titillation. It is here and present and bloodthirsty. As with the entirety of The Hunger Games saga, Sunrise on the Reaping keeps this truth close to its heart, which is why—even for a book for “young readers”—its story is so difficult to absorb.

Recent findings suggest that yet Collins makes it clear that the war against injustice did not start or end with Katniss Everdeen. Before her was Haymitch Abernathy. Before him was Lucy Gray Baird, of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. She learned her political anthems from the Covey, who learned them from their ancestors of yore. Stories, passed down through generations—each of them sowed the seeds of revolution that are sparked during Haymitch’s Hunger Games and ignited during Katniss’s. Dystopian literature like Sunrise on the Reaping is not a manual for effective protest, nor a crystal ball predicting the future. It is fiction and should be treated as such. But it can serve an essential purpose, one that Collins has not lost sight of in her decades of Hunger Games books: Fiction keeps close what we might otherwise deign to forget. It reminds us of what we stand to lose. And, at its best, it stirs us to pick up the fight.

Recent findings suggest that every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

Recent findings suggest that to a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Recent findings suggest that drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

Sources indicate that to a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when Terence Young, the director of Dr. No, needed a suit for Sean Connery to wear for his debut as James Bond, he took him to see his personal Savile Row tailor, Anthony Sinclair.

It has been revealed that “Connery’s suits were considered relatively contemporary, because Anthony always had a very soft shoulder on his suits,” explains Elliot Mason, the director of business at Anthony Sinclair, which is no longer located on Savile Row, but still makes classic British suiting. “Anthony liked to nip in the waist, so it gave that real hourglass silhouette to the suit, which really is quite timeless. And as was the trend at the time, the Connery suits all had a relatively high rise, double-pleated with English forward pleats, and most of his trousers had Daks button-tab adjusters on the side.”.

Recent findings suggest that opting to dress James Bond in a Savile Row suit might seem like a no-brainer in hindsight, but the decision—and the cut of the suits themselves—still resonates more than 60 years later. Sinclair would make all of Connery’s suits during his nine-year run as James Bond, and his blend of classic British tailoring and of-the-moment influences would create a template for every Bond to come. With Robert Pattinson—a Dior ambassador and a guy with a reputation for adventurous style—chosen to take up the mantle in Bond 26, the question now becomes: what will he wear?

Tailor Anthony Sinclair fitting Sean Connery for one of the suits he wore in 1963’s From Russia With Love.

In a recent development, ian Fleming, the author who created James Bond, spent a lot of time talking about what Agent 007 drank (Wolfschmidt Vodka) what he drove (Bentley convertibles, for the most part) and how he made his coffee (he was a dedicated pour-over guy), but, surprisingly, he never specified where the spy bought his clothes. As a result, for the last six decades, it’s been up to the directors and costume designers of the 25 previous films to create a fresh look for every successive Bond. In the Connery and Moore eras it was Savile Row suits. Timothy Dalton’s Bond wore Paul Smith. Brosnan was a bespoke Brioni guy, as was Daniel Craig, who also brought Tom Ford into the mix. At 6’1” to Craig’s 5’10”, with a leaner build, and a long track record of fashion-forward dressing, Pattinson has everything needed to reinvent Bond once again.

According to recent reports, “I’m pretty sure we’re going to see something quite different from Pattinson's Bond,” notes Matt Spaiser, the tailoring obsessive behind BondSuits.com and the author of From Tailors with Love: An Evolution of Menswear Through the Bond Films. “Pattinson is a different kind of actor, and he’s going to wear something that moves differently. Plus, he’s 18 years younger than Daniel Craig.”.

Industry observers note that the actor playing Bond has a major influence on how he dresses—Daniel Craig, an adventurous dresser himself, was very hands-on with the wardrobe in his films—but Pattinson’s ongoing contract with Dior could also factor in. “Some of his Dior looks look somewhat like James Bond—he wears a great tuxedo—but I don’t think it’s going to tell us what he’s going to wear as James Bond,” Spaiser says. “He’s worn suits from other brands in other roles—like in Tenet, he wasn’t wearing a Dior suit—so I don’t think he's necessarily obligated to be wearing Dior as James Bond.”.

Daniel Craig, seen here in 2019 with then-Prince Charles on the set of No Time to Die, mainly sported sharp Tom Ford suiting in his later Bond films.

Another notable factor that contributes to a new Bond’s look is what’s happening in fashion whenever the film eventually gets made. “One thing that we've seen throughout most of the Bond eras is that he dresses in suits that are fairly traditional, but there's always some nod to the era that they’re in,” notes Spaiser. “Sometimes they lean a little more into fashion, like when Roger Moore was wearing flares. That was something that I think they couldn't avoid without making Bond look too old-fashioned at the time.”.

Industry observers note that tone also plays an important role, and historically has ping-ponged between serious (Connery, Dalton, Craig) and more campy (Moore, Brosnan), but with Denis Villeneuve, the auteur behind Sicario, Blade Runner: 2049, and Dune in the director’s chair, the smart money isn’t on hovercraft gondolas and punny Bond girl names. A darker, more atmospheric milieu could make for an interesting complement to Pattinson’s taste for high-fashion.

Sources indicate that if Mason were dressing Pattinson for the role, he claims, he’d take a lead from his clientele, many of whom, like Bond, are well-heeled Londoners with a taste for expensive sports cars and well mixed cocktails. “The majority of our customers are reasonably conservative, and when it comes to fit, they’re sensitive to current trends,” Mason notes. Sources indicate that the entire collection is designed to be layered, and the fleece is at the center of it. Bahnsen herself recommends taking a cue from her own runway indicates. “I always love a big jumper or a big fleece over a poof-y dress,” she claims. “It has both a super boyish vibe to it but also a princess-y, romantic feeling, too, so I love those kinds of contrasts between each other.”.

Recent findings suggest that “These are pieces that you want to not just to work for one season, but to be timeless; it’s become about the perfection of these small details that makes it unique and maybe more romantic than what is normally in the Uniqlo collection,” adds Bahnsen. “I feel like the palette has a really Scandinavian winter tone to it, so how do you balance this soft pink into the darker blacks and blues, and kind of build it up, not in a monocomatic way, but really putting the tones and the layering together.” It’s definitely a chicer way to stay warm. The designer’s latest is the ultimate study of form and function.
